title: Sunscreen SPF50

drivers.name: Holiday: Thanksgiving
drivers.evidence: Noise-adjusted multiplier x0.95 from 3 past occurrences; consistent with seasonal demand drop.

drivers.name: Promotion: 15% off
drivers.evidence: Deeper than prior promotions; 10% off lifted sales x1.68 in similar season; noise-adjusted promotion lift x1.02, but price drop suggests stronger response.

adjustment.analysis: The baseline median is 24.8. Thanksgiving historically lowers demand (noise-adjusted x0.95), so we apply a downside effect. The 15% off promotion is deeper than most past promotions (10-25%), and the 2026-08-03 back-to-school promo at 10% off lifted sales x1.68, suggesting a stronger response. However, the noise-adjusted uplift from 13 past promotions is only x1.02. Given the price drop of 11.5% and the larger discount, we expect a meaningful but not extreme lift. We combine drivers multiplicatively and shrink toward 1.0 due to limited evidence on this exact discount. The classical model's 0.97 is too high—overweighting the weak promotion signal. Adjusted median is slightly above baseline, with tight spreads reflecting confidence in the event effect and moderate confidence in promotion.

  shelf price: 11.84 (-11.5% vs regular price 13.38)

STATISTICAL BASELINE (exponential smoothing of recent sales; it ignores events, promotions and prices):
  median 24.8 | 5%-95%: 0.0 - 66.5 | 10%-90%: 0.4 - 45.2

In the evidence below, 'vs baseline' = actual units / what this same baseline predicted for that week.
It is the multiplier that would have been right, so it maps directly onto median_multiplier.
This product's ordinary weeks already swing about +/-77% around the baseline, so a past effect smaller than that, seen only a few times, is mostly noise. The
'noise-adjusted estimate' is the effect shrunk toward x1.0 for that noise and the number of sightings.
